THIS  IS  not  the  first  book  of  literary  criticism  nor  is  it 
the  first  critical  work  in  Khasi  because  Khasi  literary  criti- 
cism was  born  as  early  as  192S  much  before  I was  born; 
however  the  first  work  in  book  form  was  published  only  in 
1976  which  was  follow^  by  another  in  1977. 

Literary  criticism  is  not  “book  review’*,  nor  is  it  a mere 
“appreciation”  as  Mr.  R.T.  Rymbai  held  it  in  197S.  Surely, 
no  literary  critic  would  be  prepared  to  act  as  advertising 
agent  of  authors  and  publishets.  This  book,  I believe,  will 
answer  many  of  the  questions  on  the  subject. 

At  the  time  of  writing,  one  primary  question  engaged 
my  mind:  should  I cover  all  the  major  literary  critics  or 
should  I concentrate  only  on  Khasi  critics,  or  should  I look 
only  for  a point  ? 

The  course  prescribed  by  the  previous  Board  of  Under- 
graduate Studies  for  our  Honours  students  is  too  vast  and 
vague;  The  label  ''History  of  Criticism”  immediately  tells 
a student  of  that  subject  that  it  covers  from  Plato  down  to 
F.  R.  Leavis,  and  from  the  first  Khasi  critic  down  to  the 
present  one;  Finally,  I thought  1 was  competent 
enough  to  decide  which  of  those  critics  to  be  taught  in  the 
class  and  which  ones  to  be  simply  mentioned.  But  why 
from  Plato  to  Wordsworth  only  ? Why  not  at  least  Cole-

ridge, Shelley,  Arnold,  Pater,  FJiot,  Richards  and  Leavis: 
Some  of  my  class-friends  may  have  such  question  in  mind. 

1 left  those,  as  well  as  some  Khasi  critics  for  two  reasons.  I 
have  left  out  in  this  edition  some  major  English  critics 
because  those  had  not  much  influence  on  Khasi  criticism. 
Secondly,  the  course  of  study  as  it  is  now  is  too  limited  for 
such  a scope  as  the  subject  is  only  a part  of  one  paper  at 
Honours.  On  the  other  hand,  a few  critics  of  English 
literature  may  wonder  how  Milton  comes  to  have  one  full 
chapter  in  this  book  when  even  his  fellow  countrymen  have 


ii 

not  given  him  a proper  place  in  the  history  of  criticism. 
The  reason  is  that  Milton  has  a great  deal  of  influence  on 
our  poets,  therefore,  a critical  history  of  Khasi  criticism 
would  be  somewhat  incomplete  without  him. 

This  book  is  not  a plain  history  of  criticism  because 
much  of  my  own  ciritical  tools  have  been  used  all  through. 
It  may  give  a senior  literary  historian,  who  at  a certain  place 
regards  me  as  “a  critic  of  poetry’*,  a new  food  for  thought 
It  nuy  even  change  bis  ju^ment.'  At  the  same  time  I feel 
that  my  colleagues  in  the  teaching  profession  and  in  literary 
pursuit  may,  after  studying  the  last  four  chapters,  decide 
whether  they  are  still  convinced  that  I "will  be  remembered 
by  posterity  as  the  real  harbinger  of  literary  criticism”,  as 
one  of  our  scholars  adjudged  me  in  1978. 

In  conclusion  I acknowledge  a debt  of  gratitude  to  Dr. 
R.S.  Lynsdoh  who  never  failed  to  remind  me  of  the  need  to 
have  books  on  this  subject  till  be  saw  that  I was  already 
writing  this;  to  Professor  A.G.  George  for  bis  confidence

that  the  training  he  gave  us  inside  and  outside  the  "Mayur- 
bhanj"  was  suffidenl  to  make  us  critics  of  any  literature  we 
can  read.  If  this  book  fails,  it  is  not  for  lack  of  encourage- 
ment from  them.

PREFACE  TO  THE  SECOND  EDITION 

THIS  BOOK  is  written  according  to  the  syllabus  of 
the  High  School  Leaving  Certificate  Examination.  In  pre- 
paring this  book,  care  has  been  taken  to  make  it  meet  the 
need  of  my  friends  in  Khasi  and  Jaintia  Hills  who  prepare 
themselves  for  the  HSLC  Examination  of  the  Board  of 
Secondary  Education,  Assam.  On  the  other  hand,  friends

preparing  for  one  of  the  following  examinations,  namely, 
Senior  Basic  School  Examination;  Junior  and  Senior 
Teachers’  Examination  of  the  Basic  Education  Training 
Centres  in  Khasi  - Jaintia  Hills;  and  Teachers’  Examina- 
tion of  the  Normal  Training  School,  Cherrapunjee  will  find 
this  book  indispensable. 

In  this  edition,  notes  on  six  of  the  pieces  as  translated 
by  Mr.  Tham  from  from  which  are  being  read  in 
B.A.  classes,  also  have  been  included.  Teachers  teaching 
the  pieces  treated  of  in  this  book  will  iind  it  helpful. 

The  first  edition  was  brought  out  in  1962  under  the 
title  : Matric,  Khasi  Poetry  Made  Easy:  I realise  that  some 
of  those  notes  in  the  first  edition  are  not  sufficient  to  serve 
as  answers  to  the  questions  set  in  the  examination.  What- 
ever the  standard,  in  bringing  out  the  edition,  I have  made 
myself  a pioneer  in  the  field  of  preparation  of  notes  on 
these  poems.  The  fact  that  the  present  edition  is  called  for 
shows  that  more  friends  are  added  to  me  every  year.  Rea- 
lising their  needs,  I have  included  herein  university  and 
Board  questions  on  Ka  Duitara  Ksiar  set  in  the  years  1962 
to  1966  with  model  answers. 

In  pieces  like“Kynjai  Ha  La  Ri,”  ’‘Ki  Khun  Ka 
Mariang”  and  “U  Lok  Basbisha”,  instead  of  summaries, 
substances  or  gists,  my  friends  will  on  the  other  hand  feel, 
as  if  they  were  in  my  class,  because  I deliver  a lecture  in- 
stead of  dictating  notes  to  them.

PREFACE  TO  THE  THIRD  EDITION 

THIS  BOOK  was  out  of  print  for  eleven  years.  1 
had  not  forgotten  my  readers  completely,  but  new  reasons 
overpowered  me  these  years  and  took  me  to  hitherto 
untrodden  regions  of  our  literature.  I am  confident  that 
works  produced  by  me  during  this  long  interregnum  have 
benefitted  our  Khasi  reading  public. 

This  edition  differs  greatly  from  the  second  one.  Poems 
as  were  not  composed  by  Soso  Tham,  his  translation,  and 
the  guidance  for  approaching  examination  questions  have 
all  Ixen  excluded.  New  poems  have  on  the  other  hand 
been  criticised.  I must  state  clearly  that  students  may  not

find  much  help  in  the  present  work  because  the  book  was 
prepared  with  a specific  purpose  ; to  train  the  mind  of  the 
rea^rs  for  further  research  about  the  poet.  Moreover,  the 
special  field  of  study  in  this  work  is  to  examine  the  influen* 
ce  of  other  poets  and  writers  on  Soso  Tham.  Added  to 
those  changes  effected,  a few  hundred  copies  of  the  book 
are  being  bound  with  two  others,  though  the  third  one 
which  I completed  first  is  yet  to  see  the  light  of  the  sun. 

1 suggest  to  my  readers  that  they  should  not  loose  heart 
right  now  because  they  will  in  due  course  realize  the 
importance  of  the  present  edition,  it  may  be  at  the  degree 
course,  and  it  may  be  at  the  time  when  they  prepare  for 
their  doctoral  theses  alsoi 

The  loss  of  the  earlier  features  has  been  compensated 
by  detailed  discussion  of  facts  as  those  are  revealed  to  the 
author  by  the  poems  themselves.  I am  sure  that  with  this 
edition,  the  book  will  not  escape  the  attention  of  literary 
historians  any  more.
